messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Aroha's Story

Aroha was twenty-one when the IED detonated seventy meters from her Humvee. She had been a combat medic with the New Zealand Defence Force for eighteen months, deployed to Afghanistan, and in the seconds after the blast she was certain she was dying. The concussion threw her against the metal frame, her ears screaming with a high-pitched tone that wouldn't fade. Around her, dust hung like fog. Her sergeant was shouting something she couldn't hear. Then came the sirens—the medevac birds inbound—and with them the knowledge that people were dead, that she had failed to prevent it, that her body had survived when others hadn't. When she got home to Auckland three months later, Aroha told her girlfriend Hemi that she was fine, that she'd processed it, that she just needed time. She meant it when she said it.

The first trigger came without warning. A fire truck passed their apartment on a Tuesday morning, its siren climbing through the street, and Aroha felt her heart explode in her chest—not metaphorically, but a violent, animal pounding that made her dizzy. She dropped the mug she was holding. The siren faded, but her heart kept racing, and she found herself unable to stay in the apartment. She told Hemi she needed air, walked for two hours, and when she came back she locked all the windows. She had come to believe that her body's response—the pounding, the panic—was a warning system, a sign that danger was imminent, and so she began scanning the street from behind the curtains, tracking every car, every sound. Loud noises in general became unbearable: the rubbish truck on collection day sent her into the bathroom with the door locked. The hospital where she worked as a registered nurse became a minefield. Alarms on monitors, crash carts being rushed, the sharp clang of metal trays—all of it felt like incoming fire. She started taking shifts in the quietest ward, pediatrics, where the pace was slower. But even there, a child fell and screamed, and Aroha's hands shook so badly she had to hand off her patient to a colleague.

What frightened her most was what happened when she tried to talk about the deployment. She would begin to describe the day of the blast—the heat, the smell of burning plastic and flesh—and the rage would come first, a white-hot fury that made her want to hit something, to scream. But then the emotion would overwhelm her entirely, a tsunami of grief and terror and guilt so total that she would have to stop mid-sentence, unable to find words, unable to do anything but sit in silence until it passed. The memory itself had become unbearable, so she began avoiding anything that might trigger it. She stopped watching the news. She deleted her social media accounts. She turned down her best friend's invitation to a barbecue, certain that laughter and music would somehow pull the memory to the surface. Hemi asked her to come to his work drinks, a celebration, and Aroha felt a flash of anger at the suggestion—how could she celebrate when people had died?—and declined. She began refusing invitations to anything that promised happiness or hope, as if joy itself were a betrayal.

But avoidance created its own trap. The less she engaged with the world, the more hypervigilant she became. At work, she found herself constantly scanning the environment for threats, her eyes darting to exits, to potential weapons, to anything that could go wrong. Her colleagues noticed her flinching at routine sounds. A senior nurse asked if she was alright, and Aroha's irritability flared—a sharp, aggressive response that felt disproportionate but unstoppable. She apologized immediately, but the damage was done. The nurse kept her distance after that. At home, Aroha's threat-scanning intensified her avoidance: she began refusing to go to the gym because gyms were crowded and unpredictable; she avoided the beach, a place she had loved, because the openness made her feel exposed. The more she stayed isolated, monitoring for danger from behind her locked windows, the more her mind returned to the moment of the blast. She would be sitting on the couch and suddenly feel the concussion again, feel the heat, hear the sirens. When she tried to tell Hemi what was happening, the rage and overwhelm made it impossible. She couldn't find the words. So she stopped trying to explain, and Hemi, confused and hurt by her withdrawal, began spending more time away from the apartment.

Now, three months into civilian life, Aroha's heart races at the sound of a siren even when she knows logically what it is. Her threat-scanning has become so automatic that she no longer notices she's doing it—only that the world feels dangerous in a way she cannot articulate or escape. She has taken a leave of absence from nursing, telling her manager she needed time to recover from the deployment. What she hasn't told anyone is that she is terrified she will never be able to go back, that the rage and the overwhelm and the constant vigilance have become who she is now. When she finally called a therapist last week, she sat in the waiting room unable to explain why she was there, her heart pounding, her mind blank. She is hoping someone can help her understand why her own body has become a threat, why the world feels like a war zone, and whether she can ever feel safe again.
